claims.text: The initial eutectic AlCoCrFeNi-system alloy has a dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure.
Weak interlamellar boundaries in the initial alloy tend to initiate microcracks during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Adding approximately 0.2 wt% boron will promote boron segregation to lamellar-colony boundaries.
The boron addition and proposed thermal processing will form thin boride-enriched interfacial layers at dual-phase lamellar boundaries.
Casting followed by homogenization near 1100°C for several hours and controlled cooling will facilitate interfacial boron segregation without extensive continuous boride formation.
Boron preferentially segregates to internal boundaries.
Interfacial boron enrichment reinforces boundary cohesion.
The proposed interfacial chemical modification delays microcrack nucleation under tensile loading.
The proposed interfacial chemical modification delays microcrack propagation under tensile loading.
Boron treatment may refine the interlamellar-boundary structure.
Delayed cracking and stronger interfaces allow the alloy to sustain higher stress before failure.
Delayed cracking and stronger interfaces allow the alloy to sustain greater strain before failure.
The boron-treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The boron-treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
The unmodified conventionally processed eutectic alloy typically exhibits high strength at the expense of ductility because of weak interlamellar boundaries.
Excessive continuous boride networks would deteriorate tensile ductility.
Higher boron concentrations or overly aggressive cooling may produce unwanted brittle phases.
Boron segregation is known to strengthen grain and interface boundaries in alloy systems other than the proposed eutectic HEA.
